prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

NASS and U.S. Crop Production Forecasts: Methods and Issues

April 13, 2017 R44814

The National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) estimates agricultural production (including area and yield) and stocks for more than 120 crops and 45 livestock items. Traditionally NASS estimates have focused on state and national data, but in recent years county-level estimates have gained in importance. NASS crop production estimates are crucial to people in the U.S. agricultural sector involved in making marketing and investment decisions, policymakers who design farm support programs, USDA agents who implement those programs, and producers who benefit from those programs.

NASS conducts hundreds of surveys every year and prepares reports covering many aspects of U.S. agriculture. For example, NASS survey data are used to produce forecasts of area, yield, production, value, and stocks for major crop and livestock products, as well as for estimates of the historical number of farms and land in farms, land rental rates and values, farm labor usage, fertilizer and chemical usage, computer usage and ownership on farms, and farm production expenditures. NASS also undertakes a National Census of Agriculture every five years that provides comprehensive information about the nation’s agriculture down to the county level. The census includes data on the number of farms, land use, production expenses, value of land and buildings, farm size and characteristics of farm operators, market value of agricultural production sold, acreage of major crops, inventory of livestock and poultry, and farm irrigation practices.

NASS spending is controlled by annual appropriations acts. In FY2016, Congress appropriated $177 million for NASS operations, including $126.2 million (75% of its budget) for annual agricultural estimates and $42.2 million (25%) for the Census of Agriculture.

The critical role that NASS data plays in promoting a smooth and efficient marketing process for U.S. agriculture makes NASS’s successful function a concern of Congress. In particular, three issues related to NASS’s survey methodology and crop estimates are of potential concern to Congress. First, a trend has emerged since the early 1990s of declining NASS survey response by farmer participants. For most crops, NASS production estimates are based on data collected from farm operations via grower survey responses. The quality of NASS crop acreage and production estimates depends on a high level of participation by agricultural producers. As the number of respondents falls, the statistical reliability of estimates and forecasts declines and the value of NASS estimates for a host of other purposes declines as well.

The second issue derives primarily from the first in that the declining survey response impacts more localized or regional estimates first, particularly county-level estimates and those programs that are based on county-level data. In particular, insufficient response rates in some counties have led to unexpectedly wide discrepancies across counties in farm program payment rates under the county-based revenue support program—Agricultural Risk Coverage (ARC-CO)—established under the 2014 farm bill (P.L. 113-79). These discrepancies have generated concern about whether the new revenue program is working as intended or whether this is simply a data problem that needs to be addressed. Barring any near-term fix by USDA, lawmakers may elect to address county-to-county payment disparities in the context of the next farm bill.

Third, market participants and policymakers alike are concerned that NASS estimates be unbiased and objective so as not to influence market prices or volatility. Analysis of NASS data suggests that it is both objective and trustworthy; however, variability of data as measured by market price reactions to NASS estimates appears to have increased in recent years.

Summary

The National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) estimates agricultural production (including area and yield) and stocks for more than 120 crops and 45 livestock items. Traditionally NASS estimates have focused on state and national data, but in recent years county-level estimates have gained in importance. NASS crop production estimates are crucial to people in the U.S. agricultural sector involved in making marketing and investment decisions, policymakers who design farm support programs, USDA agents who implement those programs, and producers who benefit from those programs.

NASS conducts hundreds of surveys every year and prepares reports covering many aspects of U.S. agriculture. For example, NASS survey data are used to produce forecasts of area, yield, production, value, and stocks for major crop and livestock products, as well as for estimates of the historical number of farms and land in farms, land rental rates and values, farm labor usage, fertilizer and chemical usage, computer usage and ownership on farms, and farm production expenditures. NASS also undertakes a National Census of Agriculture every five years that provides comprehensive information about the nation's agriculture down to the county level. The census includes data on the number of farms, land use, production expenses, value of land and buildings, farm size and characteristics of farm operators, market value of agricultural production sold, acreage of major crops, inventory of livestock and poultry, and farm irrigation practices.

NASS spending is controlled by annual appropriations acts. In FY2016, Congress appropriated $177 million for NASS operations, including $126.2 million (75% of its budget) for annual agricultural estimates and $42.2 million (25%) for the Census of Agriculture.

The critical role that NASS data plays in promoting a smooth and efficient marketing process for U.S. agriculture makes NASS's successful function a concern of Congress. In particular, three issues related to NASS's survey methodology and crop estimates are of potential concern to Congress. First, a trend has emerged since the early 1990s of declining NASS survey response by farmer participants. For most crops, NASS production estimates are based on data collected from farm operations via grower survey responses. The quality of NASS crop acreage and production estimates depends on a high level of participation by agricultural producers. As the number of respondents falls, the statistical reliability of estimates and forecasts declines and the value of NASS estimates for a host of other purposes declines as well.

The second issue derives primarily from the first in that the declining survey response impacts more localized or regional estimates first, particularly county-level estimates and those programs that are based on county-level data. In particular, insufficient response rates in some counties have led to unexpectedly wide discrepancies across counties in farm program payment rates under the county-based revenue support program—Agricultural Risk Coverage (ARC-CO)—established under the 2014 farm bill (P.L. 113-79). These discrepancies have generated concern about whether the new revenue program is working as intended or whether this is simply a data problem that needs to be addressed. Barring any near-term fix by USDA, lawmakers may elect to address county-to-county payment disparities in the context of the next farm bill.

Third, market participants and policymakers alike are concerned that NASS estimates be unbiased and objective so as not to influence market prices or volatility. Analysis of NASS data suggests that it is both objective and trustworthy; however, variability of data as measured by market price reactions to NASS estimates appears to have increased in recent years.

NASS and U.S. Crop Production Forecasts: Methods and Issues

Introduction

The United States is one of the world's largest producers and exporters of major field crops including wheat, rice, coarse grains (corn, barley, sorghum, and oats), oilseeds (soybeans, peanuts, canola, sunflowers, and other minor oilseeds), and cotton. Unexpected changes in the outlook for production of a major U.S. crop can lead to sharp movements in both domestic and global market prices. If sustained, large price volatility can lead to significant resource adjustments in the agricultural sector and possibly to large changes in outlays under U.S. farm support programs.1

The potential for market disruptions and financial loss led to the creation of a statistical bureau within the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) in 1863, just a year after USDA was established. This statistical bureau eventually became the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS). NASS and its USDA precursors were created to provide independent, objective, reliable, timely, and accurate market information for the agriculture industry.2

Report Overview

This report provides an overview of NASS. First, it reviews the origins, legislative authority, and funding for NASS. Then, the report describes the survey methodology used by NASS to generate crop production forecasts and estimates for U.S. crops at both the state and national level. Third, this report describes the systematic evolution that occurs over the course of a growing season for both the survey methodology and the annual sequence of NASS reports that are used to convey the crop production forecasts to the U.S. agricultural sector. Fourth, this report describes how NASS survey methodology is extended to collect county-level crop area and yield estimates. This fourth section also includes a discussion of emergent issues related to low producer response rates to NASS surveys and the subsequent discrepancies in neighboring county yield estimates and farm program payments. Finally, the report discusses how evidence on market price reaction to USDA crop production forecasts indicates that there is no visible pattern of bias or error.

Congressional Interest

NASS conducts a series of surveys throughout the year to assess farmer planting decisions and production outcomes. The resulting NASS crop production and stock estimates underlie USDA and private analysis that affects markets throughout the year. They provide a benchmark in the marketplace because of their comprehensive nature, objectivity, and timeliness. For example, NASS estimates provide the foundation for USDA's global commodity supply and demand balance sheets published in the monthly World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report.3

The public benefits of NASS data are notable, and the literature on those benefits was recently reviewed by the Council on Food, Agricultural and Resource Economics, which highlighted how public information on market prices and quantities helps improve market efficiency.4 NASS data are considered crucial to both policymakers in government and those making marketing and investment decisions, as well as to the design and implementation of U.S. farm support programs.5 The reliability and accuracy of USDA's crop supply and demand estimates play a prominent role in the smooth function of agricultural commodity supply chains, including forward contracting, stock management, and commodity futures exchanges. This reliability helps to ensure a more informed and stable marketplace.

The quality of NASS crop acreage and production estimates depends on a high level of participation by agricultural producers. In recent years declining grower response rates to NASS surveys have diminished the statistical reliability of NASS estimates. In particular, low response rates to NASS surveys in some counties have led to unexpected and inconsistent farm program payment rates under the new county-based revenue support program—Agricultural Risk Coverage (ARC-CO)—established under the 2014 farm bill (P.L. 113-79). This issue is discussed in more detail in the section "Increasing Nonresponse Degrades County Yield Calculations" of this report. These discrepancies have generated considerable concern about whether the new revenue program is working as intended or whether this is simply a data problem that needs to be addressed. Barring any near-term fix by USDA, lawmakers could elect to address county-to-county payment disparities in the context of the next farm bill.

NASS Overview

NASS's mission statement states that the agency "provides timely, accurate, and useful statistics in service to agriculture."6 In fulfillment of this mission, NASS collects and publishes current national, state, and county agricultural statistics. NASS is also responsible for administration of the Census of Agriculture, which occurs every five years and provides comprehensive data on the U.S. agricultural economy.7

NASS is one of four agencies—along with the Agricultural Research Service, the National Institute of Food and Agriculture, and the Economic Research Service—in USDA's agricultural research, education, and extension mission area.8 NASS is headquartered in Washington, DC,9 but maintains a network of 12 regional offices, including a National Operations Center in St. Louis, MO, and 50 state field offices through cooperative agreements with state departments of agriculture or universities.10

NASS survey data are used to produce forecasts of area, yield, production, value, and stocks for major crop and livestock products, as well as for estimates of the historical number of farms and land in farms, land rental rates and values, farm labor usage, fertilizer and chemical usage, computer usage and ownership on farms, and farm production expenditures.11 In addition to the several hundred nationally focused statistical reports from its headquarters each year, NASS state statistical offices issue some 9,000 reports and news releases annually that highlight or expand on information from the national reports.12 In addition, NASS conducts and releases the Census of Agriculture every five years.

In support of this work, NASS maintains a fairly comprehensive working list of farms and ranches in the United States, one of its unique federal roles. NASS also performs important reimbursable agricultural survey work for other federal agencies, state governments, and producer organizations and provides technical assistance for agricultural statistics programs in developing countries.

National Operations Center (NOC)

Among its activities, NASS's NOC houses the National Operations Division (NOD). NOD is responsible for several critical survey support activities, including maintenance of the list sampling frame, interviewer training for both field and telephone enumerators, centralized data collection via telephone interviewing (NOD has 154 calling seats and conducted over 1.1 million telephone calls in 2015), and processing of the paper-based survey questionnaires that are completed and returned by mail from farmers and ranchers.13 In 2015, the Forms Processing Group at NOD handled over 436,000 forms. It also processes a significant portion of the Objective Yield Samples collected by field personnel from winter wheat, corn, soybean, and cotton field plots.

Information Quality

NASS operations are guided by an Advisory Committee on Agriculture Statistics.14 The purpose of the committee is to advise the Secretary of Agriculture on the scope, timing, content, etc., of the periodic censuses and surveys of agriculture, other related surveys, and the types of information to obtain from respondents concerning agriculture. The committee also prepares recommendations regarding the content of agriculture reports and presents the views and needs for data of major suppliers and users of agriculture statistics.

In addition to guidance from the committee, NASS is subject to USDA's Information Quality Guidelines that apply to any information disseminated by NASS.15 The guidelines emphasize the confidentiality of respondents and objectivity of analysis.

Annual Data Users' Meeting

Annually, NASS—in coordination with the World Agricultural Outlook Board (WAOB), ERS, Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS), Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS), and the U.S. Census Bureau—hosts a meeting of key data users. The annual Data Users Meeting provides an open forum for data users—both government and nongovernment—to ask questions and provide feedback about the entire USDA statistics program, including data products from NASS.16

At the 2016 meeting held in Chicago on October 18, the Farm Service Agency (FSA) participated for the first time and addressed questions about NASS county-level data availability, particularly in relation to the issues that emerged with regard to payments under the ARC county-level program. This issue is discussed in more detail in the section "County-Level Crop Production Estimates" of this report.

NASS Operating Authority

NASS's responsibilities are authorized under the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 (7 U.S.C. 1621-1627) and the Census of Agriculture Act of 1997 (P.L. 105-113; 7 U.S.C. 2204g).17 Under this broad authority and the discretion of the Secretary, NASS exists and performs its data collection and dissemination functions in support of the U.S. agricultural sector.18 In particular, because of its transparent and objective methodology, NASS data contribute to the orderly association among the consumption, supply, marketing, and input sectors of agriculture.

Over the years, various other laws have designated specific authority to the Secretary for data collection and publication regarding particular commodities and reports.19 These include laws concerning the collection of agricultural production and price data for apples

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Crop Production
Description: The USDA Crop Production report, released monthly by the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS), provides official estimates on U.S. agricultural acreage, yield, and production for major field crops, fruits, and nuts.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the USDA NASS Crop Production report comprehensively. Let me start with several searches covering different angles.Excellent start. The CRS report looks very useful. Let me fetch it and search for more on history and methodology.I have strong material on history and authority. Now let me research data access channels, confidentiality rules, users, and recent developments.Very helpful. Now let me research confidentiality law, the lockup/embargo system, and preservation/archival access.The search limit is reached, but I can still fetch pages directly. Let me pull key NASS pages on confidentiality and regulations.Let me get details on the Agricultural Statistics Board lockup procedures, which is a key part of the dataset's integrity regime.# The USDA Crop Production Report: A Comprehensive Research Profile

**Verification of your description:** Your description is accurate. The *Crop Production* report is indeed released monthly by USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS) and provides official U.S. estimates of acreage, yield, and production. Two refinements worth knowing: (1) during the growing season the report publishes *forecasts* (e.g., "based on conditions as of September 1"), which are revised after harvest and finalized years later; and (2) while the report's core is major field crops (corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton, sorghum, rice, oats, barley, peanuts, etc.), fruits, nuts, hops, and maple syrup content appears seasonally in specific months' issues rather than in every report. The report is issued under the seal of the **Agricultural Statistics Board (ASB)**, NASS's official estimating body. It is one of USDA's eight "principal federal economic indicator" reports (per USDA budget documents, NASS produced six of the eight: Agricultural Prices, Crop Production, Grain Stocks, Cattle on Feed, Hogs and Pigs, and Acreage).

---

## 1. Publisher and Organizational Context

- **Agency:** National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS), an agency of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), within the Research, Education, and Economics (REE) mission area (alongside the Agricultural Research Service, Economic Research Service, and National Institute of Food and Agriculture).
- **Mission statement:** NASS "provides timely, accurate, and useful statistics in service to agriculture" — often branded "The Fact Finders of U.S. Agriculture."
- **Structure:** Headquarters in Washington, DC; a National Operations Center in St. Louis, MO (which handles centralized telephone data collection, questionnaire processing — over 436,000 forms in 2015 — and the list sampling frame); 12 regional offices; and ~50 state field offices operating through cooperative agreements with state departments of agriculture and land-grant universities. State offices collectively issue roughly 9,000 reports and releases annually.
- **The Agricultural Statistics Board:** Every *Crop Production* report is signed out by the ASB — a permanent chairperson, secretary, and rotating NASS subject specialists who review survey data and "set" the official estimates under secure "lockup" conditions before release. The ASB is the institutional custodian of the estimates' officialness.

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

NASS's authority is layered across a century and a half of statutes:

- **Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946** (7 U.S.C. 1621–1627): the principal operating authority for agricultural statistics and estimation, delegating to the Secretary the collection and dissemination of agricultural data "to improve the operating efficiency of agricultural markets."
- **7 U.S.C. 2204 (and 476, 951):** general authority under which the Secretary collects crop and livestock statistics and prepares official estimates; implemented through the delegation at **7 CFR 2.68** to the NASS Administrator ("Prepare crop and livestock estimates and administer reporting programs... Prepare reports of the Agricultural Statistics Board... covering official state and national estimates").
- **Census of Agriculture Act of 1997** (P.L. 105-113; 7 U.S.C. 2204g): transferred the Census of Agriculture from the Commerce Department to USDA/NASS, conducted every five years (years ending in 2 and 7). Census data underpin the sampling frames and final benchmark revisions for the Crop Production series.
- **Confidentiality law (2008 Farm Bill provisions, 7 U.S.C. 2276; 18 U.S.C. 1902):** individual respondent data are protected by law; unauthorized disclosure is a federal crime. This is the legal foundation of NASS's confidentiality pledge and of respondent trust.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act:** every survey behind the report (e.g., OMB control numbers like 0535-0212, 0535-0109) must carry OMB clearance; PRA actions were the formal vehicle for recent program discontinuations.
- **Information Quality Act / USDA Information Quality Guidelines and the E-Government Act of 2002** (§207(f) web publishing schedules) also govern how the data are disseminated.

## 3. History

The Crop Production report is arguably the oldest continuously running federal statistical product in agriculture:

- **1840:** The first Census of Agriculture provided the first nationwide production inventory.
- **1862:** President Lincoln establishes USDA — "the People's Department" — with statistics collection as one of its two original duties.
- **July 10, 1863:** USDA's Division of Statistics issues its first monthly crop condition report, promising a report on the 10th of every month. NASS traces its founding to this date. The original rationale: commodity buyers had better market information than isolated farmers; federal statistics would level the playing field for price discovery. Also strategically important for supplying Civil War armies.
- **1866:** Annual statistics on crop production, livestock, and farm prices begin — the data series behind today's "Track Records" extends back to 1866 for corn, wheat, cotton, oats, barley, hay, and other crops.
- **1905:** A scandal involving advance knowledge of crop forecasts leaked to a New York cotton speculator leads to creation of the **Crop Reporting Board** and the secure **lockup system** — the ancestors of today's ASB and release procedures.
- **1961:** USDA reorganization creates the **Statistical Reporting Service (SRS)**.
- **1986:** SRS renamed the **National Agricultural Statistics Service**; Crop Reporting Board renamed the **Agricultural Statistics Board**.
- **1997/1998:** Census of Agriculture responsibility transfers from Commerce to NASS.
- **2024–2026:** Period of budget-driven program cancellations and restorations (see §8).

## 4. Content, Methodology, and Release Practices

- **Frequency and timing:** Monthly, on pre-announced release dates (typically mid-month, e.g., Jan 12, Feb 10, Mar 10, Apr 9, May 12, Jun 11, Jul 10, Aug 12, Sep 11 in 2026), generally at 12:00 noon ET. Release dates are published in a NASS reports calendar far in advance — a deliberate market-integrity feature.
- **What it contains:** National and state-level estimates/forecasts of planted acreage, harvested acreage, yield, and production for principal field crops; seasonal specialty-crop content (fruits, nuts, hops, maple syrup, potatoes, dry beans); monthly weather and agricultural summaries in some issues. Example headline: the September 11, 2026 issue forecast corn for grain at 15.8 billion bushels (second-highest on record) at 178.5 bu/acre.
- **Survey machinery:** The report draws on multiple probability surveys — quarterly acreage/production/stocks surveys (June Area Survey, March/June/September quarterly crops surveys), farmer-reported yield surveys, and **Objective Yield surveys** in which enumerators physically measure plants and fruit counts in randomly selected field plots (corn, soybeans, cotton, wheat) across sample states. Remote sensing (Cropland Data Layer) is used in acreage estimation.
- **Forecast vs. estimate lifecycle:** In-season numbers are forecasts; after harvest, estimates are revised through the January **Crop Production Summary** (annual), and commodity estimates are not considered "final" until after the next Census of Agriculture (e.g., 2023–2024 estimates finalize after the 2027 Census). NASS publishes **Track Records** documenting each vintage of every estimate against the final figure — an unusually transparent revision-audit trail. Typical forecast accuracy: July/August forecasts land within roughly 3–13% of the final number depending on the year and crop.
- **WASDE linkage:** Crop Production numbers feed directly into USDA's monthly *World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates* (WASDE), released simultaneously the same day under joint lockup.

## 5. Data Access and Formats (for data librarians and scientists)

- **Report files:** Each monthly issue is distributed as PDF, TXT, and ZIP through NASS's site and, more importantly for preservation, through **ESMIS** — the USDA Economics, Statistics, and Market Information System at Cornell's Mann Library (esmis.nal.usda.gov), which archives issues going back decades and offers email subscriptions.
- **Quick Stats database** (quickstats.nass.usda.gov): the comprehensive query tool for all published NASS estimates — national, state, and county levels, with data for many series back to the 1800s. *Quick Stats Lite* offers simplified structured queries.
- **Bulk downloads:** Daily-updated gzipped flat files at nass.usda.gov/datasets — the full crops file is over 1 GB; separate files for census years, animals, economics, demographics.
- **REST API** (quickstats.nass.usda.gov/api): free API key, JSON/XML/CSV output, filtering by commodity/geography/time with comparison operators, 50,000-record cap per request. The **rnassqs** R package (rOpenSci) wraps the API for reproducible, automated research workflows — well documented in the *Journal of Open Source Software*.
- **Complementary products:** Track Records; Statistical Bulletins (final estimates, 1987–2012); Census of Agriculture archive; CroplandCROS/Cropland Data Layer (satellite-derived acreage geodata); ASB Executive Briefings; Price Reactions studies.
- **Rights and reuse:** As works of the U.S. federal government, the reports and data are in the **public domain** (17 U.S.C. 105), freely reusable without license restrictions, though NASS requests citation credit and maintains a formal citation-request convention.

## 6. Typical Users and Uses

- **Commodity markets:** Grain merchandisers, exporters, processors, analysts, and futures traders treat release days as market events; academic and NASS "Price Reactions" studies document measurable CME price movement around each report. The CRS finds no visible pattern of bias — the estimates are regarded as objective and trustworthy benchmarks.
- **USDA policy machinery:** WASDE balance sheets, FSA farm-program administration (county ARC-CO revenue-support payments are computed directly from NASS yields), and RMA crop insurance all depend on the series.
- **Producers:** For marketing, planting, and investment decisions — fulfilling the original 1863 mandate of giving farmers information parity with buyers.
- **Researchers and data scientists:** Economists, agronomists, climate researchers (long yield histories back to 1866 are valuable for trend and climate-impact analysis), and journalists.
- **Global audiences:** As the reference standard for world crop supply, via WASDE and FAS export reporting.

## 7. Public Benefits

- **Market efficiency and price discovery:** Independent analysis (reviewed by the Council on Food, Agricultural and Resource Economics) confirms public price-and-quantity information improves market efficiency; the CRS notes NASS data ensure "a more informed and stable marketplace" supporting forward contracting, stocks management, and futures markets.
- **Program integrity:** Farm bill programs (ARC-CO, PLC, crop insurance, disaster aid) require credible, objective yield/production benchmarks to function fairly.
- **Transparency and anti-manipulation:** The lockup system and pre-announced schedules prevent insiders from profiting from early access — the direct lesson of the 1905 leak scandal.
- **Coverage scale:** NASS estimates production for 120+ crops and 45 livestock items; the Crop Production program is the flagship of that portfolio.

## 8. Risks, Controversies, and Current Concerns (policy-activist and preservationist view)

- **Declining survey response rates** since the early 1990s degrade statistical reliability, hitting county-level estimates first — and county estimates directly drive ARC-CO payment rates, producing anomalous payment disparities between neighboring counties (a recurring CRS-flagged congressional concern).
- **Budget-driven cancellations and restorations:** In April 2024, NASS cancelled the July Cattle report, the Cotton Objective Yield Survey, and **all County Estimates for Crops and Livestock** due to an ~11% budget cut (~$7.5M would have been needed to restore them). After congressional appropriations language, they were reinstated in March 2025. In August 2025, NASS discontinued the Mink and Agricultural Labor surveys under PRA "efficiency" provisions, and eliminated state/regional reports.
- **Workforce erosion:** The American Statistical Association's "Nation's Data at Risk" reporting documents that NASS lost an estimated **41% of its staff** between FY2024 and 2025 (probationary terminations, deferred resignations, buyouts), with multiple acting or vacant leadership positions as of late 2025.
- **Funding trend:** NASS appropriations have eroded in real terms for years — roughly $177M (FY2016), ~$187.9M (FY2025, same as FY2024), with an FY2026 request of ~$185M — an estimated 14.5% purchasing-power loss since FY2009. Government shutdowns (e.g., November and December 2025) have forced rescheduling of reports, breaking the pre-announced-release integrity norm.
- **Preservation posture:** Fortunately, this dataset is unusually well-archived: ESMIS at Cornell mirrors the full report series in PDF/TXT/ZIP; Quick Stats retains the full estimate history including superseded revisions; Track Records preserve every vintage; and the historical archive extends to 19th-century publications. The principal preservation risks are program discontinuation (data simply stops being collected, as nearly happened to county estimates) and API/dissemination-platform changes.

## 9. Key Sources Consulted

CRS Report R44814, "NASS and U.S. Crop Production Forecasts: Methods and Issues" (2017); 7 U.S.C. 2204g, 7 CFR 2.68, and P.L. 105-113; NASS official pages (History of Agricultural Statistics; ASB and Lockup; Regulations Guiding NASS; Datasets; Quick Stats/developer pages); NASS *Crop Production* and *Crop Production 2025 Summary* reports and Track Records; ESMIS/Cornell Mann Library; NASS ASB Notices (2024–2025); American Statistical Association "The Nation's Data at Risk" (2025); USDA Explanatory Notes FY2025; Agri-Pulse, DTN, and AgWeb coverage of report cancellations; rOpenSci **rnassqs** documentation.

**Bottom line:** The Crop Production report is a 160-year-old public statistical institution — the direct descendant of the USDA's very first 1863 monthly crop report — legally grounded in the Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946, protected by some of the strictest confidentiality and embargo rules in the federal statistical system, and indispensable to commodity markets, farm policy, and the public's interest in a transparent food system. Its greatest present threats are not technical but budgetary and political.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

I'll research recent developments affecting NASS, its staffing, funding, and the Crop Production report specifically.I've found critical information about the 2025 shutdown impacts. Let me research the ICR/Federal Register status and historical data availability.I have strong evidence for most categories. Let me verify the leadership situation and the specialty-crop survey discontinuations that directly affect Crop Production content.# Risk Assessment: USDA NASS Crop Production Report

**Assessment date context:** Research conducted October 2026. This assessment covers developments since January 2025, including the record 43-day federal shutdown (October 1 – November 12, 2025) and the administration's workforce-reduction actions.

---

## Historical Data Availability

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- The full run of historical *Crop Production* issues remains publicly accessible. The release archive (release.nass.usda.gov) and the migrated ESMIS archive at the National Agricultural Library (esmis.nal.usda.gov) both serve past issues; historical report files dating back decades remain downloadable.
- Quick Stats retains the complete historical estimate series — the query tool offers data back to the 1860s–1870s, and the bulk download files (e.g., qs.crops, 1.05 GB) were last refreshed October 8, 2026, indicating the historical database is actively maintained.
- No evidence of any prior-year *Crop Production* issue or data element being deleted or altered.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- The ESMIS archive, hosted at Cornell's Mann Library since the 1990s, was **decommissioned October 1, 2025** and migrated to USDA's National Agricultural Library (Reuters, Sept. 30, 2025). The content was preserved, but the access location changed abruptly — a warning sign for link rot and access continuity, and it moved the archive from a university partner back solely to federal infrastructure.
- The 2024 production-year **county estimates for crops and livestock were never collected or published** (cancelled April 2024), creating a permanent gap year in the county-level historical record for crop production data (restored only beginning March 2025).

**Finding: No Known Issue.** For the dataset as defined — the monthly *Crop Production* report series — all prior files remain publicly available without known alteration. However, the ESMIS migration and the permanent 2024 county-estimate gap are genuine watch items that keep this category near the Moderate boundary.

---

## Future Data Availability

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- The **October 9, 2025 *Crop Production* report was never released.** NASS's November 19, 2025 notice stated plainly: "Crop Production (Oct. 9) will not be released." NASS officials later confirmed some shutdown-skipped reports "will not be revisited or released" — the October 1 yield forecasts are permanently absent from the historical record. Under the rubric, "publication skipped" is explicitly a High Risk trigger.
- The November 2025 report was delayed from November 10 to November 14 due to the lapse in appropriations (NASS notice, Oct. 31, 2025) — also a "typical publication date missed" event.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk" (i.e., why not lower):**
- The December 2025 and all 2026 issues (through September 2026) were released on the pre-announced schedule.
- The underlying ICRs are active: the Field Crops Production collection (OMB No. 0535-0002) had a substantive-change renewal submitted to OMB in October 2026 (adding sugarcane questions), and the Objective Yield Surveys ICR (OMB No. 0535-0088) was approved by OIRA on February 20, 2026, expiring June 30, 2027 — no expiration lapses.

**Finding: High Risk.** A full monthly issue was permanently skipped in 2025 and another was delayed — squarely matching the rubric's High Risk definition ("collection or publication skipped"). The 2026 on-time record and active ICRs prevent escalation but do not cure the skipped publication.

---

## Data Quality

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- **Reductions in collection frequency/granularity within this report's scope:** The April 2026 Objective Yield renewal (Federal Register, 2026-06978) includes the **discontinuation of the California Almond and Oregon Hazelnut objective yield surveys** and a **reduction of Florida Citrus survey waves from 12 to 5** — directly degrading the fruit/nut forecasts published in *Crop Production*.
- The November 2025 ASB Executive Briefing confirmed that "because the October 2025 Crop Production report was not published, there are no October 1 yield forecasts included in this report" — missing data points within the series.
- The 43-day data blackout produced "the widest range of analyst estimates in a decade for corn and soybean yields" (Reuters, Nov. 13, 2025), demonstrating degraded information quality during the gap.
- County-level crop estimates were entirely absent for the 2024 production year.
- Long-declining farmer survey response rates (flagged by CRS since 2017) plus a ~40% staff reduction create ongoing risk to estimate reliability; state and regional context reports that supplemented national data were eliminated in 2025.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- Core field-crop coverage (corn, soybeans, wheat, cotton) continues at full monthly frequency and national/state granularity; 2026 reports appear methodologically unchanged.

**Finding: High Risk.** There have been actual, implemented reductions in granularity and frequency of data feeding this report (specialty-crop objective yield eliminations, citrus wave cuts, a permanently skipped issue, and a missing monthly yield forecast), not merely emerging threats.

---

## Statutory Context

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- Authority is explicitly named and clear: 7 U.S.C. 2204 ("The Secretary of Agriculture shall procure and preserve all information concerning agriculture which he can obtain... by the collection of statistics"), quoted verbatim in the active Field Crops Production ICR; implementing delegation at 7 CFR 2.68; Agricultural Marketing Act of 1946 (7 U.S.C. 1621–1627); confidentiality governed by 7 U.S.C. 2276 and CIPSEA.
- Required for implementation of federal programs: production estimates are used by the Secretary to administer farm program legislation and import/export programs (stated in the ICR), feed WASDE, and underpin FSA/RMA program administration.
- No comprehensive substitute exists: private forecasters (analyst polls, ag-data firms) cannot replace official, confidentiality-protected probability-survey estimates; NASS's own budget justification warns that absent federal data, market information "would be exclusively controlled by a limited number of entities" exposing markets to manipulation.

**Evidence for "Moderate/High Risk":**
- The monthly publication cadence is not tied to a hard statutory deadline, and Congress has shown willingness to let NASS cancel reports (April 2024) when funding falls short — statutory authorization does not guarantee appropriation.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** This is the dataset's strongest category: explicit statutory authority, clear collection mandate, essential federal-program use, and no true substitute.

## Staffing and Funding

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- **Staff loss of ~40%:** The American Statistical Association's "Nation's Data at Risk" reporting estimates NASS lost **41% of its staff** from FY24 to FY25 (39.5% per OPM data; DTN reported 275 departures, ~34%, from deferred resignations, probationary terminations, and retirements). USDA's own FY2027 budget notes confirm a reduction from 754 to 489 staff-years.
- **Leadership hollowing:** As of November 2025, the associate administrator is serving in an acting capacity, three of six administrator's-office units have acting directors (two have no one in charge), and four of seven divisions are headed by acting directors — three of whom double up on two divisions each. The USDA Chief Economist (who oversees WASDE, released jointly with *Crop Production*) resigned effective January 2026.
- **Structural upheaval:** The administration announced plans to disperse NASS staff to five USDA "hubs," consolidating its 12 regional offices.

**Evidence for "Moderate/No Risk" elements:**
- Budget: FY2025 enacted $187.9M; FY2026 enacted ~$185M — only a ~1.5% nominal cut (well under the 10% threshold), though purchasing power is down an estimated 14.5% since FY2009.
- Career Administrator Joseph Parsons remains in place (appointed June 2024), providing continuity at the top.

**Finding: High Risk.** The staff-loss threshold (≥40% by the most-cited estimate, 34–39.5% by conservative counts, combined with pervasive acting leadership and a forced reorganization) clearly meets the High Risk bar even though the topline budget cut is small.

## Policy

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- **Administration-priority-driven eliminations implemented in 2025–2026:** NASS's August 28, 2025 notice discontinued the Mink and Agricultural Labor surveys and eliminated state and regional reports, stating the action was "taken under the provisions of the Paperwork Reduction Act as part of the government's efforts to improve efficiency" — explicitly framed around administration efficiency priorities.
- USDA budget documents state NASS "has reorganized its internal operations and functions to align with the administration's priorities."
- The April 2026 ICR revision discontinued almond and hazelnut objective yield surveys and cut citrus collection waves — administration-efficiency-driven changes that directly reduced what this report collects and publishes.
- The October 2025 issue was lost to a shutdown driven by the administration's funding standoff, and NASS reports were suspended during it.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- The core monthly field-crop report itself was never targeted for elimination; it is politically protected by its market-criticality. The July Cattle report and county estimates, cancelled in April 2024, were **restored in March 2025** after congressional appropriations language — evidence that Congress actively defends these programs.

**Finding: High Risk.** Significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities have actually been implemented (survey discontinuations, report eliminations, collection-frequency cuts affecting this report's specialty-crop content), which matches the rubric's High Risk language. A defensible alternative reading is Moderate, since the flagship field-crop estimates continue untouched — but the pattern of executed, policy-driven reductions across NASS's portfolio, including inputs to this very report, supports High.

## Summary of Risk Levels

Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue** (with watch items: ESMIS archive migration off Cornell; permanent 2024 county-estimate gap)
Future Data Availability: **High Risk** (October 2025 issue permanently skipped; November 2025 delayed; ICRs currently active)
Data Quality: **High Risk** (almond/hazelnut objective yield discontinued; citrus waves cut 12→5; missing October 1, 2025 yield forecasts)
Statutory Context: **No Known Issue** (explicit 7 U.S.C. 2204 authority; essential to federal program administration; no substitute)
Staffing and Funding: **High Risk** (~34–41% staff loss; widespread acting leadership; regional-office consolidation; budget roughly flat)
Policy: **High Risk** (implemented administration-efficiency-driven discontinuations across NASS programs, including inputs to this report; core field-crop report continues)

**Overall assessment:** The *Crop Production* report is statistically and legally robust — its statutory foundation, archived history, and market-critical status make outright termination unlikely — but it is operating inside a severely degraded institution. The 2025 shutdown demonstrated that a full monthly issue can be permanently lost, and administration-efficiency actions have already chipped away at the report's specialty-crop granularity. The most probable failure mode is not deletion but erosion: skipped or delayed issues, thinned coverage at the margins, and reduced estimate reliability from a ~40%-smaller workforce.

**Key sources:** NASS ASB Notices (Oct. 31, Nov. 19, Dec. 22, 2025; Aug. 28, 2025); NASS/USDA FY2026 and FY2027 Explanatory Notes; ASA "The Nation's Data at Risk" (2025 and 2026 Midyear Update); Reuters (Sept. 30 and Nov. 13, 2025); Federal Register notices 2026-00542, 2026-06978, 2026-20237; reginfo.gov ICR records (0535-0002, 0535-0088); DTN/Progressive Farmer (Dec. 22, 2025); National Sustainable Agriculture Coalition; CRS Report R44814; NASS Data Users' Meeting Q&A (2024).
